title: A Scribe with a King's Letter
sum: Nearly sixty years after the temple was finished, a new figure arrives: Ezra, a priest whose family tree climbs to Aaron and a scribe expert in the law of Moses. In the seventh year of King Artaxerxes he leads a company of Israelites, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants from Babylon to Jerusalem, a four-month journey made safe, the narrator says, because God's good hand was on him. The reason for it all is given in one verse: Ezra had set his heart to search out the LORD's law, to do it and to teach it (7:10).

Then the language changes to Aramaic for a copy of the king's letter. Artaxerxes lets any Israelite who wishes go with Ezra, sends gifts of silver and gold, orders the treasurers of Beyond the River to supply him, frees the temple staff from taxes, and gives Ezra power to appoint judges and teach the law, with the empire's penalties behind it. The chapter ends in Hebrew and in the first person: Ezra blesses the God who put this in the king's heart.
readings: Most historians accept that a Jewish priest-scribe came from Babylon with royal backing in the Persian period, and the letter's style and Persian loanwords fit the chancery of the time. The questions are which Artaxerxes sent him, how much of the letter is the king's own wording, and what the law in his hand contained (see below and the notes on 7:1, 7:14 and 7:26).
Read as the opening of a new act

Ezra–Nehemiah tells its story in movements: the return and the temple (1–6), Ezra and the law (7–10), Nehemiah and the wall (Nehemiah 1–7), and the community gathered around the law (Nehemiah 8–13). Chapter 7 echoes chapter 1: a Persian king moved by God, a decree, gifts for the house of God, and volunteers going up. Tamara Eskenazi reads the book as the story of a community, in which the house of God grows from a building into a people shaped by the law.

views.H: Ezra is a real priest and scribe sent by Artaxerxes I in 458 BC, and the letter is a copy from the royal files, perhaps drafted with Jewish help. The repeated "hand of God" (7:6, 7:9, 7:28) explains how a pagan king came to fund the temple: God moves rulers' hearts, as he moved Cyrus's.
views.C: Critical scholars debate the date (458 or 398 BC), the letter's authenticity and the identity of the law. Some, such as Lester Grabbe, doubt that a Persian king would write so much Jewish theology; others, such as H. G. M. Williamson, accept a genuine core reworked by Jewish editors. Charles Torrey's view that Ezra was a literary invention has few followers today.
views.A: The letter is a showcase of Persian administration: the title "king of kings," the seven counselors, the province Beyond the River, treasurers (gizzabrayya), Persian loanwords such as asparna, tax exemptions for temple staff, and the pairing of a god's law with the king's law. Parallels include the Udjahorresnet inscription from Egypt and the Elephantine letters.
views.J: The rabbis saw Ezra as a second Moses: "Ezra was worthy that the Torah be given through him, had Moses not come before him" (Bavli Sanhedrin 21b). Resh Lakish said that when the Torah was forgotten in Israel, Ezra came up from Babylon and restored it (Bavli Sukkah 20a). Verse 7:10 (seek, do, teach) became a model for the life of a sage.
views.X: Christian writers honored Ezra as a restorer of Scripture; Irenaeus says that after the exile Ezra, inspired by God, set the words of the prophets in order again (Against Heresies 3.21.2). The scribe who studies, lives and teaches the law anticipates Jesus' "scribe who has learned to be a disciple of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 13:52), and Ezra's journey of faith without an armed escort (8:22) became a favorite example of trust in providence.

deep.b:
Ezra 7:7–8 dates Ezra's arrival to the seventh year of "Artaxerxes the king." The book places him before Nehemiah, who came in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I, 445 BC (Nehemiah 2:1), and Nehemiah 8–12 shows them together. Three dates are argued.

458 BC (Artaxerxes I). The traditional view and probably still the majority view among commentators, including Williamson and Blenkinsopp. It takes the text's order at face value, fits Egypt's revolt of about 460–454 BC as a reason for royal interest, and explains the joint appearances in Nehemiah. Kidner and Williamson add Meremoth son of Uriah, the priest who weighs Ezra's treasure (8:33) and repairs two sections of the wall under Nehemiah in 445 BC (Nehemiah 3:4, 3:21): that fits a career that ran from 458 to 445 far better than one from 445 to 398.

398 BC (Artaxerxes II). Proposed by Albin van Hoonacker in 1890 and championed by H. H. Rowley. Arguments: Ezra meets a large population in Jerusalem (10:1), while Nehemiah found the city nearly empty (Nehemiah 7:4); Ezra uses the room of Jehohanan son of Eliashib (10:6), apparently the high priest known from the Elephantine letter of 407 BC; Ezra thanks God for a "wall" (9:9); and Nehemiah's memoir never names Ezra outside passages many think were edited in. To the Meremoth argument Rowley replied that the name was common and the treasurer of 8:33 could be a later man of the same priestly family.

428 BC (the 37th year of Artaxerxes I). John Bright suggested that "seventh" lost a digit, which would make Ezra Nehemiah's younger colleague. No manuscript supports the change.

Each answer has replies: "wall" can be a figure (see the note on 9:9), Jehohanan may be a different man or the room named later, and Jerusalem's population need not match a gathering from all Judah. The question is open.

The letter is written in Imperial Aramaic and uses the forms and Persian words of the period, which convinced scholars such as Eduard Meyer and, later, Williamson that it rests on a real document. Its Jewish features (detailed sacrifices, the singers and gatekeepers, the phrase "the God of Israel, who makes his home in Jerusalem") are explained either by Jewish drafters who prepared it for the king's seal, as Udjahorresnet did for his own mission in Egypt, or by later editing. Skeptics, including Lester Grabbe, think the scale of the gifts and the sweeping powers given to Ezra show a Jewish composition. A middle view is common: a genuine commission, preserved in a form shaped by the community that treasured it.

echoes: Ezra 1:1–4; Ezra 6:6–12; 1 Chronicles 6:3–15; Nehemiah 2:1–9; Nehemiah 8:1–12; Psalm 45:1; Isaiah 60:7–13; Matthew 13:52

settings.to: The returned community, for whom priestly descent decided who could serve (2:61–63)
settings.why: To show Ezra's right to act as a priest: his line runs through Zadok, Phinehas and Eleazar to Aaron. The list is shortened compared with 1 Chronicles 6 (see the note on 7:3), which shows that its purpose is to prove a link, not to give every generation.

settings.by: Artaxerxes, king of Persia (as the copy presents him)
settings.to: Ezra the priest and scribe, in Babylon; from 7:21 the decree also addresses the royal treasurers of the province Beyond the River
settings.when: Before Ezra's departure, in the king's seventh year (458 BC on the usual dating; 398 BC on another)
settings.why: To authorize the journey and anyone willing to join it, to transfer funds and supplies, to exempt temple staff from tax, and to give Ezra power to appoint judges and teach the law with royal penalties behind it. Read as a document handed to Ezra, it is his warrant: something he could show to governors and treasurers along the way. Copied into the book, it tells Jewish readers that the empire itself stood behind the law.
views: Most scholars accept a genuine commission in Persian chancery style, perhaps drafted by Jewish officials for the king's seal.
Some think it was composed or heavily expanded by Jewish writers to give the law and the temple imperial authority.

settings.to: God, and the readers of his memoir
settings.when: On receiving the king's letter, as he gathers family heads for the journey
settings.why: To give the credit for the king's favor to the God of Israel and to open the memoir with praise. It tells readers how to read the letter they have just heard: not as Persian generosity alone, but as God's loyal love at work through a king.

title: The Road from Babylon
sum: Ezra lists the heads of the families who traveled with him: two priestly houses, a descendant of David, and twelve lay families, about 1,500 men. At the Ahava canal he finds no Levites, so he sends to Iddo at Casiphia, and 38 Levites and 220 temple servants join the caravan. Ezra had told the king that God protects those who seek him, so he is ashamed to ask for soldiers. Instead he calls a fast, and God answers.

He weighs out an enormous treasure of silver, gold and fine vessels to twelve priests and twelve Levites, telling them that they and the vessels are holy. After about four months they reach Jerusalem safely. The gifts are weighed again and recorded, the returned exiles offer sacrifices for all Israel, and the king's orders are delivered to the satraps and governors, who support the people and the temple.
readings: The departure in the first month, the fast for "a straight road," the gathering of Levites to carry holy things, and the safe arrival echo Israel's march from Egypt and Isaiah's promise of a new exodus from Babylon (Isaiah 40:3; Isaiah 52:11–12). The offerings for "all Israel" in multiples of twelve show a people reconstituted as the twelve tribes.

The chapter has the dry exactness of an official record: names, numbers, weights and dates. Ezra was responsible for royal and community funds, and the careful weighing at both ends (8:25–30, 8:33–34) reads like an accounting to his sponsors as much as to God.

views.H: Ezra's refusal of an escort is an act of faith that God honored. The care for Levites and holy vessels shows a leader who wanted the temple served exactly as the law prescribed.
views.C: Critics note the stylized numbers (twelve families, offerings in twelves) and the very large treasure, and suspect that the memoir's numbers were inflated or schematized. The two missing clan names in 8:5 and 8:10 show the Hebrew list was damaged in copying; the Greek fills them in.
views.A: Persian-period details abound: the canal camp in Babylonia, darics (the gold coin of Darius I), satraps and governors of Beyond the River, and the use of royal orders on the road. The Murashu archive from Nippur shows Jews living by Babylonian canals in this very period.
views.J: Jewish tradition read Ezra's insistence on Levites and on proven lineage as part of his purification of the people; the Talmud says he left Babylon only after making it "like fine flour" (Bavli Kiddushin 69b). The fast at the Ahava became an example of fasting before a dangerous journey.
views.X: Christian preachers have often set Ezra's refusal to ask the king for soldiers (8:22) beside Nehemiah's escort (Nehemiah 2:9) to discuss faith and prudence. The holy men guarding holy things (8:28) has been applied to ministers entrusted with the gospel (1 Timothy 6:20; 2 Timothy 1:14).

echoes: Ezra 2:1–70; Numbers 4:1–20; Exodus 12:1–6; Isaiah 40:3; Isaiah 52:11–12; Nehemiah 2:9; 1 Chronicles 3:19–22; 1 Chronicles 24:1–6

settings.to: The returned community in Judah and the readers of the memoir
settings.when: Recording who made the journey with him
settings.why: To show that the new arrivals belonged to known families of Israel, most of them already represented in the first return (Ezra 2), and to give each house its place in the restored people.

settings.what: The fast and plea at the Ahava
settings.to: God, with the whole caravan, men, women and children, fasting together at the Ahava canal
settings.when: Before setting out, after the Levites had joined (8:15–20)
settings.why: To ask God for a safe road for the people, their children and their goods, since Ezra had refused to ask the king for an armed escort. Ezra reports that God was moved by their pleading, and the safe arrival (8:31) is told as the answer.

settings.what: Ezra's earlier words to the king
settings.when: Before the journey, as Ezra reports it
settings.why: A public claim about God's protection that Ezra could not then undercut by asking for soldiers. Knowing it was said to a pagan king explains Ezra's shame: his God's honor was at stake before the empire.

settings.to: The twelve chief priests and the twelve Levites chosen to carry the gifts (8:24)
settings.when: At the Ahava camp, as the silver, gold and vessels are weighed out to them
settings.why: To make them answerable for every item until it is weighed again in the temple storerooms, and to remind them that holy things belong in holy hands (Numbers 4:15).

title: Ezra's Prayer
sum: After the journey, officials report that the people, priests and Levites included, have not kept apart from the peoples of the lands. They have married their daughters, so that the holy seed has mingled with them, and leaders were first in this unfaithfulness. Ezra tears his clothes, pulls out his hair and sits stunned until the evening offering, while those who tremble at God's word gather around him.

Then he kneels, spreads out his hands and prays. He confesses the people's guilt from their ancestors' day to the present, thanks God for the brief favor of a remnant, a tent peg in the holy place, and kindness from the kings of Persia, and admits that they have broken the commands God gave through the prophets: not to marry the peoples of the land. He asks nothing. He ends by placing the guilty people before a righteous God.
readings: The prayer stands with Nehemiah 9 and Daniel 9 as a model of corporate repentance. Ezra, who had not married a foreign wife, says "we" throughout, and he lays the case before God without excuses or requests.

The prayer is said aloud at the temple, in front of a gathering crowd (10:1). Many readers notice how it works on its hearers: it names the sin, recalls the exile, raises the fear of total destruction (9:14), and prepares the way for the drastic proposal of chapter 10. On this reading Ezra's prayer is also a sermon.

views.H: Ezra faithfully applies God's law to a real danger: a small community absorbing the religion of its neighbors through marriage, as Israel had done before (Judges 3:6; 1 Kings 11:1–4).
views.C: Scholars note how the officials' list combines Deuteronomy 7 and 23 and how the prayer's "quotation" weaves together several Torah texts (Fishbane). Many also ask whether the "peoples of the lands" included Judeans who had never gone into exile, which would make the crisis partly about land and status (Smith-Christopher; Eskenazi and Judd).
views.A: Marriage between communities was common across the Persian Empire; the Elephantine papyri record Jews in Egypt marrying Egyptians and Arameans. Ezra's demand for separation stands out against that background.
views.J: The rabbis drew from these chapters rules on marriage and descent, and found room for Ruth in Deuteronomy 23 (see the note on 9:12). The "tremblers" (charedim) of 9:4 gave their name to ultra-Orthodox Jews today.
views.X: Christian readers have admired the prayer's humility and its solidarity with sinners, a pattern they see fulfilled in Christ who bore others' guilt. Many have also struggled with its demand for separation, setting it beside Paul's counsel not to leave an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:12–14), while others apply it to the warning against being yoked with unbelievers (2 Corinthians 6:14).

deep.h: The marriages: four ways of reading
deep.b:
Preserving a small community's faith. Many commentators (Kidner, Williamson, Fensham) stress the danger: a few thousand returnees surrounded by larger peoples, whose children were already losing the language of Judah (Nehemiah 13:24). Marriage meant joining families, gods and land. Without a firm line, they argue, the community that carried the Scriptures would have dissolved within a generation.

Holiness by descent. Christine Hayes argues that Ezra introduces a new idea, "holy seed," which made Israelite descent itself holy and closed the door to conversion by marriage. Later Judaism did not follow this to the end: it welcomed converts.

Ethnic and social exclusion. Others, such as Daniel Smith-Christopher and Tamara Eskenazi with Eleanore Judd, think many of the "foreign" women were from families that had stayed in the land, and that the returnees were defining who counted as Israel and who could inherit. Harold Washington, David Janzen and Willa Johnson press the ethical case: no law commands divorce, Deuteronomy 23:7–8 admits Egyptians whom 9:1 bans, the women are never said to worship other gods, and the cost fell on women and children with no voice in the text (see the note on 10:3).

In tension with other Scriptures. Joseph married an Egyptian (Genesis 41:45), Moses a Midianite and a Cushite (Exodus 2:21; Numbers 12:1), Boaz the Moabite Ruth, who said "Your people are my people, and your God is my God" (Ruth 1:16). Isaiah 56:3–7 tells foreigners who join themselves to the LORD not to fear being separated from his people, and calls the temple a house of prayer for all peoples. Some scholars, such as André LaCocque, think the book of Ruth was told, or retold, as an answer to Ezra; others date Ruth earlier and see the tension within the canon itself. The Bible keeps both voices.

echoes: Deuteronomy 7:1–6; Deuteronomy 23:3–8; Leviticus 18:24–30; Isaiah 6:13; 1 Kings 8:46–50; Nehemiah 9:6–37; Daniel 9:4–19; Nehemiah 13:23–27; Ruth 1:16; Isaiah 56:3–7

settings.to: Ezra, who had come with royal authority to teach and judge by the law (7:25)
settings.when: Some months after his arrival (compare 7:9 and 10:9)
settings.why: To bring a problem to the man empowered to deal with it. The report is already an interpretation: it applies the old lists of Canaanite and excluded nations (Deuteronomy 7:1; Deuteronomy 23:3–7) to present neighbors and calls the marriages sacrilege (ma'al). Its admission that officials led the way shows the reformers were confessing their own class's guilt.

settings.to: God, the LORD of Israel; said aloud at the temple, before the tremblers who had gathered and, as he prayed, a growing crowd of men, women and children (9:4; 10:1)
settings.when: At the time of the evening offering, after sitting stunned for hours
settings.why: To confess the community's guilt as a whole and leave its fate with God. On many readings it also teaches the crowd how to see their situation and moves them to act; it is answered not by God's voice but by Shecaniah's proposal (10:2–4).
views: Derek Kidner reads it as a sincere prayer of repentance that happens to be overheard; its power over the crowd is the fruit of its honesty.
Addressed to the people as well
H. G. M. Williamson notes that it is spoken aloud before a gathering crowd and prepares them for the hard decision of chapter 10, a public act of leadership as well as a prayer.

Those who think the Ezra memoir was composed or heavily shaped by a later writer, as Charles Torrey argued, read the prayer as a literary composition that teaches the book's readers how to understand the crisis.

settings.by: God, "through your servants the prophets" (Moses and his successors)
settings.to: Israel about to enter the land
settings.when: Recalled by Ezra from Leviticus 18 and Deuteronomy 7 and 23
settings.why: In its first setting the law forbade alliances and marriages with the nations of Canaan so that Israel would not be drawn to their gods. Ezra applies it to a new people in a new century, which is itself an act of interpretation.

title: Wives Sent Away
sum: As Ezra weeps before the temple, a great crowd gathers and weeps with him. Shecaniah son of Jehiel confesses for the people and proposes a covenant to send away the foreign wives and their children, and urges Ezra to act. Ezra makes the leaders swear, fasts in a temple room, and a proclamation summons every man of the exile to Jerusalem within three days, on pain of losing his property and his place in the community.

In December's cold rain the men of Judah and Benjamin sit in the temple square. Ezra tells them to confess and separate themselves; they agree, but ask for a slower process. Four men oppose it, or perhaps oversee it. A court of family heads works for three months, and the book ends with the names of the men who had married foreign women, priests first, and a hard closing line about wives and children.
readings: The chapter follows the pattern of earlier reforms: confession, a covenant sworn before God, a public assembly, and action according to the law (compare 2 Kings 23:1–3; Nehemiah 10:28–31). On this reading the community chose painful obedience to keep its faith alive.

Other readers start with those the text leaves silent: the women, who are never named, and the children, whose fate is not told. The book ends not with a celebration but with a list and a broken sentence (10:44), which some take as a sign that the narrator, too, felt the cost.

views.H: The reform was necessary and successful in the short term, though the problem returned under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 13:23–27). The leaders acted by consensus and process, not by force alone.
views.C: The third-person narrative may come from the editor rather than Ezra's memoir. Scholars debate who the women were (see the note on 10:2), whether the list records all cases or only a few (about 113 men), and whether the dismissals actually happened, since the Hebrew of 10:44 does not say so.
views.A: The power to confiscate property and expel members (10:8) matches the authority the royal letter gave Ezra (7:26), and the court of family heads fits local self-government under Persian oversight.
views.J: Rabbinic law took several principles from the chapter: a court's power over property (10:8; Bavli Yevamot 89b), and, linked to Deuteronomy 7:3–4, the rule that a child's status follows the mother. Later law also held that a marriage with a non-Jew had no legal force (Bavli Kiddushin 68b), which removed the need for divorce.
views.X: Most Christian traditions do not take 10:3 as a model for believers, pointing to Paul: a believer should not leave an unbelieving spouse who is willing to stay, and the children are holy (1 Corinthians 7:12–14). Some read Ezra as guarding the line through which the Messiah would come; others see in the church's welcome of the nations the answer to the tension Ezra left (Ephesians 2:14).

deep.b: Shecaniah's covenant includes "the children born of them" (10:3). Nothing in the Torah orders this, and nothing in the text says how the women and children lived afterward. The verb is not the ordinary word for divorce, and no certificate is mentioned (Deuteronomy 24:1). Commentators who defend the reform argue that the children would naturally stay with their mothers' families, that the alternative was the community's loss of its identity, and that the process was slow and judicial (10:13–17). Critics, among them Harold Washington, David Janzen and Willa Johnson, note that women and children paid the price for decisions made by men, that Isaiah 56:3 uses the very verb of 10:11, badal, to promise the foreigner that the LORD will not separate him from his people, and that the Bible elsewhere protects divorced women and orphans (Deuteronomy 24:1–4; Exodus 22:22). Malachi 2:13–16 condemns men who break faith with the wives of their youth, and some scholars read it as a voice from the same period protesting such divorces, though others think Malachi addresses a different situation. The ending of the book in Hebrew (10:44) leaves the reader with the children, not with a report of success.

deep.title: Claude's reading: an ending left open on purpose
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. The book could have ended with a report that the men obeyed, as 1 Esdras 9:36 does. Instead the Hebrew ends with names and with children (10:44), and Nehemiah 13 shows the same problem a generation later. I read this as deliberate restraint: the narrator records the community's decision without celebrating it, and hands the reader the human cost in the last words. The same book had earlier held a door open to outsiders (see the note on 10:11). The main published explanation of the abrupt ending is different: it is a seam. If Nehemiah 8 once followed Ezra 10, as in 1 Esdras, or stood between Ezra 8 and 9, as Torrey and Williamson argue (see the note on 9:1), then the ending was made when the material was moved, not chosen by a narrator. My reading survives that only in part: whoever made the seam still left the Hebrew's last words about wives and children in place, where 1 Esdras closes with a report of obedience. It overlaps with Tamara Eskenazi's argument that the book's lists are part of its design, not filler, a way of putting the whole community by name at the center; but the claim that ending on this list signals unease is mine.
deep.refs: Ezra 6:21; Ezra 10:11; Ezra 10:44; Nehemiah 7:73–8:12; Nehemiah 13:23–27; 1 Esdras 9:36

echoes: Deuteronomy 7:3–4; Deuteronomy 24:1–4; Leviticus 5:15; Joshua 7:19; 1 Chronicles 28:10; Nehemiah 10:28–31; Nehemiah 13:23–31; Malachi 2:10–16; 1 Corinthians 7:12–14

settings.by: Shecaniah son of Jehiel, of the clan of Elam, whose own family may have been involved (10:26)
settings.to: Ezra, in front of the weeping crowd at the temple
settings.when: While Ezra lies prostrate in prayer
settings.why: To turn confession into action: a covenant to send away the wives and children, with Ezra leading. Coming from a layman of an implicated family, it showed the reform had support from within the guilty group itself, and it gave Ezra a mandate.

settings.to: All the people of the exile in Judah and Jerusalem
settings.why: To summon every man within three days, under threat of losing his property to the temple and being cut off from the community. It uses the powers granted in the king's letter (7:26) to make the assembly binding.

settings.to: The men of Judah and Benjamin assembled in the temple square, in the rain
settings.when: The twentieth day of the ninth month
settings.why: To name the sin, call for confession and order separation from the peoples of the land and the foreign wives. Spoken to men who had married, it asks them to break up their own households; their answer (10:12–14) shows assent mixed with practical reluctance.
To accept the decision while asking for a workable process: officials acting for the assembly and cases heard town by town with local elders and judges.

settings.what: The list of men with foreign wives
settings.by: The narrator, from the court's records
settings.when: After the hearings ended on the first day of the first month
settings.why: To record publicly who was found guilty, starting with the high priest's family. Read with the hard last line (10:44), the list also preserves the fact that real families and children were affected.

traditions.q: Ezra had the men send away their foreign wives (Ezra 10:3, 10:11). May a Christian marry an unbeliever, and may such a marriage be ended?
views: A Catholic may marry an unbaptized person only with the bishop's permission (Code of Canon Law 1086). A marriage between two baptized people that is valid and consummated cannot be dissolved, but under the Pauline privilege a convert whose unbaptized spouse leaves may marry again (canons 1143–1147; 1 Corinthians 7:15).

The Council in Trullo (692) forbade an Orthodox Christian to marry a heretic and said such a marriage must be dissolved, yet, following Paul, it said that if two unbelievers marry and one comes to faith, they should not part (canon 72). Today the Orthodox Church blesses marriages with baptized Christians of other churches but not with the unbaptized. It may allow a divorce and second marriage out of pastoral mercy (economy).

Christians should marry only in the Lord (Westminster Confession 24.3). Divorce is allowed only for adultery or for desertion that cannot be remedied (24.6), so a believer may not leave a willing unbelieving spouse.

Believers should marry believers (2 Corinthians 6:14), and marriage is a lifelong covenant (Baptist Faith and Message 18). Baptists differ on whether divorce for adultery or desertion frees a person to marry again, and do not take Ezra's dismissals as a pattern for the church.
